hook: SCP-701 is written like a scholar's dossier on an obscure seventeenth-century revenge tragedy, complete with a publication history and a list of surviving editions. It helps to know that plays of this kind traditionally end in a final act strewn with bodies. The horror here is not a creature on the loose but a production that slowly and politely goes wrong, so pay attention to the rehearsal timeline.
whyItMatters: As its tags show, the article belongs to the wiki's Hanged King and Alagadda material, and the title figure enters here through the medium of theatre. It tells a memetic-hazard story through stage history and book collecting instead of a lab report, which gives the threat the dusty weight of something that has been circulating for centuries. The page itself points to an incident report and the play's text as separate documents, so this main file reads as the overview of a larger set.
thingsToNotice: The outbreak pattern is laid out like a production calendar: a week or two out, the cast start performing a different version of the script in perfect unison and insist it has always gone that way; by the end of Act I a strange figure is standing at the edge of the stage; in the Act V banquet it is written into the play as the Hanged King. At that point the actors kill each other or themselves, sometimes with props that were not there a moment earlier, and the audience riots, attacking whoever happens to be in front of them; survivors who leave keep up the violence for about a day, and some end up comatose or permanently psychotic. That only about a third of productions end this way keeps the threat unpredictable. The publication history shows a text that refuses to stay buried, turning up under other titles online and as photocopies in school drama departments. The closing exchange delivers the bleakest line: the Overseer turns down the Keter upgrade and calls it lucky to lose only a hundred or so people a decade, because the secret got out long ago.
